questions.question: In a vehicle routing problem, one vehicle must visit five locations, and every trip starts and ends at the depot, where refuelling is possible. The range limit is 100 miles per trip, and the shortest single tour through all five locations is 130 miles long. What follows?
options: The problem has no feasible plan, since 130 exceeds 100.
The plan must use at least two trips, returning to refuel.
The vehicle may refuel at the fifth location to finish the tour.
The farthest location is dropped, so one tour can be kept.

questions.question: A vehicle can travel at most 100 miles between refuelling stops, and it can refuel only at the depot. A routing plan consists of several trips, each leaving and returning to the depot. To which distances does the 100-mile limit apply?
options: To the total distance of the whole plan.
To each single leg between two of the locations.
To the length of each depot-to-depot trip.
To the one-way distance to each location.

questions.question: In a vehicle routing problem (shortest total distance; every location visited; every depot-to-depot trip within the range limit), the range limit is dropped and the new problem is solved exactly. Why is its optimal distance a lower bound on the original optimum?
options: Every original plan is still allowed, so the new minimum cannot be larger.
Dropping the limit removes long trips, so the remaining plans are all shorter ones.
The new optimal plan respects the range too, so both optima are equal.
The relaxed problem has fewer locations, so its plans cover a shorter distance.

questions.question: A routing plan currently serves locations $A$ and $B$ with two separate depot round trips. A planner considers replacing them by one trip depot $\to A\to B\to$ depot, which is shorter in total. When is this change allowed?
options: Whenever $A$ and $B$ are the two closest locations to the depot.
Whenever the new trip is shorter than both separate trips together.
Only when no other location is visited after $B$.
Only when the joined trip stays within the range limit.

questions.question: In a vehicle routing problem with a range limit per trip, the heuristic plan visits every location on its own depot round trip, and every such round trip is within the range. What does the plan's total distance guarantee?
options: It is the minimum total distance, since each trip is a direct round trip.
It is a lower bound, since joining visits can only add extra distance.
It is an upper bound on the minimum distance, not proof of optimality.
It is a valid bound only after the range limit has been removed.

questions.question: A vehicle has a range of 100 miles per trip and refuels only at the depot $D$. The distances are $D$ to $P$: 30 miles, $P$ to $Q$: 25 miles, and $Q$ to $D$: 40 miles. Is the trip $D\to P\to Q\to D$ allowed?
options: No, since it serves two locations without a refuelling stop.
Yes, since its length is 95 miles, within the range.
Yes, since its length is 55 miles, within the range.
No, since the trip plus the return to the depot needs $95+40=135$ miles.

questions.question: For a vehicle routing problem that seeks the shortest total distance, two feasible plans of 150 and 120 miles are known, and the problem without the range limit has optimal distance 85 miles. Which interval for the optimal distance $z^*$ is the tightest that this information guarantees?

A plan serves $X$ (14 miles from the depot) and $Y$ (22 miles from the depot) on two separate round trips; $X$ and $Y$ are 11 miles apart. They are joined into one trip depot $\to X\to Y\to$ depot, which is within range. By how many miles does the plan's total distance fall?
options: 11 miles
36 miles
47 miles
25 miles

questions.question: For a vehicle routing problem that seeks the shortest total distance, a heuristic plan of 180 miles is feasible, and the problem without the range limit has optimal distance 165 miles. What does this show about the heuristic plan?
options: It is exactly 15 miles longer than the best feasible plan.
It is at most 15 miles longer than the best feasible plan.
It is optimal, since 180 is an upper bound on the optimum.
It must be improved, since the optimum is 165 miles long.

questions.question: In a vehicle routing problem with a range limit per trip, the range limit is dropped and the resulting problem is solved exactly. Its optimal plan turns out to respect the range limit on every trip. What follows for the original problem?
options: The plan is optimal for the original problem.
The plan only gives a lower bound on the optimum.
The plan is feasible but may be improved.
The plan is optimal only if no heuristic is shorter.

questions.question: In a vehicle routing problem with a range limit per trip, the problem without the range limit is solved, and its optimal plan has a trip that exceeds the range. Must the original optimal distance be strictly larger than the relaxed optimal distance?
options: Yes, since the relaxed plan is infeasible, its distance is unattainable.
Yes, since a plan respecting the range must make extra depot returns.
No, since another plan may respect the range at the same distance.
No, since the original optimum is always the smaller one.

questions.question: For a vehicle routing problem that seeks the shortest total distance, the range limit per trip is lowered from 100 to 80 miles while everything else stays the same. How can the optimal total distance change?
options: It can only fall, as trips must be shorter.
It stays the same, since the locations have not changed.
It must rise, since every 100-mile plan becomes infeasible.
It can rise or stay the same, but it cannot fall.

questions.question: Locations $U$, $V$, $W$ are served from depot $D$. Distances: $D$-$U$ 10, $D$-$V$ 12, $D$-$W$ 15, $U$-$V$ 8, $V$-$W$ 9, $U$-$W$ 16 miles. When the range limit per trip is ignored, what is the minimum total distance of a plan that starts and ends at $D$ and visits all three?
options: 37 miles
27 miles
42 miles
74 miles

questions.question: A vehicle refuels only at the depot and has a range of 100 miles per trip. One required location $E$ is 55 miles from the depot, and no route between them is shorter. What can be said about the vehicle routing problem?
options: It is infeasible: any trip visiting $E$ is at least 110 miles.
It is feasible, since the 55 miles to $E$ are within the 100-mile range.
It is feasible if $E$ is visited in the middle of a longer trip.
It is feasible once $E$ is moved to the end of the last trip.

questions.question: For a vehicle routing problem that seeks the shortest total distance, the problem without the range limit has a correctly computed optimum of 202 miles. A colleague reports a plan of 195 miles in which every trip is within the range. What follows?
options: The plan is optimal, since it beats the relaxed bound.
The plan must break another rule, such as skipping a location.
The plan is consistent, since 202 is an upper bound.
The relaxed bound applies only to plans that violate the range.

questions.question: For a vehicle routing problem (shortest total distance; visit every location; every trip within 100 miles; refuel only at the depot), which modified problem does not have an optimal value that is guaranteed to be a lower bound on the original optimum?
options: Raise the range limit to 150 miles per trip.
Allow refuelling at the locations as well as the depot.
Lower the range limit from 100 to 80 miles per trip.
Drop the range limit and keep all other requirements.

questions.question: Depot $D$ serves $A$, $B$, $C$ with range 70 miles per trip. Distances: $D$-$A$ 20, $D$-$B$ 25, $D$-$C$ 30, $A$-$B$ 15, $B$-$C$ 20, $A$-$C$ 35 miles. What is the minimum total distance of a feasible plan?
options: 150 miles
85 miles
115 miles
120 miles

questions.question: For a vehicle routing problem that seeks the shortest total distance, a feasible plan has 214 miles. Relaxation 1 has optimum 190 miles; relaxation 2 has optimum 197 miles, and a non-optimal feasible solution of relaxation 2 has 205 miles. Which interval for the optimal distance $z^*$ is the tightest guaranteed?
